clinicalPearls: A disorder of symmetrical, disproportionate subcutaneous adipose accumulation affecting the buttocks, hips and legs and sometimes the arms, occurring almost exclusively in women.
Onset or worsening clusters around periods of hormonal change, notably puberty, pregnancy and the menopause, pointing to an oestrogen-related influence.
The feet are characteristically spared, producing an abrupt cuff or bracelet at the ankle, in contrast to lymphoedema which typically involves the foot.
The affected tissue is tender and painful, and patients bruise easily owing to increased capillary fragility.
The Stemmer sign is negative in early disease and the swelling is non-pitting, helping to separate it from lymphoedema.
The disproportion is resistant to dietary energy restriction and generalised weight loss, which reduce visceral and upper-body fat while sparing the affected depots.
Longstanding lipoedema may cause secondary lymphatic overload, producing lipo-lymphoedema with foot involvement and a positive Stemmer sign.
It is frequently misdiagnosed as simple obesity, causing considerable psychological distress and inappropriate blame for perceived dietary failure.
reference.pathophysiology: Lipoedema is characterised by hyperplasia and hypertrophy of subcutaneous adipose tissue in a symmetrical, gynoid distribution that spares the trunk, hands and feet. The precise mechanism is incompletely understood, but proposed contributors include a hormonally modulated adipose disorder, microangiopathy with increased capillary permeability and fragility (accounting for pain and bruising), altered adipocyte and extracellular matrix behaviour, and a hereditary predisposition given frequent familial clustering. In early disease lymphatic transport is preserved, but progressive adipose expansion mechanically overloads the lymphatics and may culminate in secondary lymphatic insufficiency (lipo-lymphoedema). Chronic inflammation within the expanded fat and low-grade tissue oedema are thought to sustain symptoms.
additionalDifferentials: systemic oedema from cardiac, renal or hepatic disease
additionalInvestigations: clinical assessment of distribution, tenderness, bruising and Stemmer sign
lymphoscintigraphy where lymphoedema or lipo-lymphoedema is suspected
venous duplex ultrasonography to exclude venous disease
dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry or bioimpedance for body composition
thyroid, renal, hepatic and cardiac evaluation to exclude systemic causes
high-resolution ultrasound of subcutaneous tissue to gauge fat thickness
redFlags: new pitting oedema and a positive Stemmer sign indicating secondary lymphatic failure
skin breakdown, recurrent cellulitis or lymphorrhoea
features of a coexisting eating disorder or severe psychological distress
rapidly progressive or asymmetrical swelling prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Lipoedema is a chronic, often slowly progressive condition that is not corrected by diet alone; conservative measures such as compression, exercise and complex decongestive therapy control symptoms, and liposuction can achieve durable reduction of affected fat in selected patients. Progression to lipo-lymphoedema worsens the outlook if untreated.
pitfalls: labelling the condition as simple obesity and attributing failure to lose the affected fat to poor adherence
confusing it with lymphoedema and applying the wrong management emphasis
overlooking evolution into lipo-lymphoedema when the foot becomes involved
neglecting the pain, bruising and psychological burden that define the patient experience
expecting bariatric or dietary weight loss alone to resolve the disproportion
references: Wold, Hines and Allen description and subsequent lipoedema consensus guidance
International Society of Lymphology Consensus Document on peripheral oedema
management: No pharmacotherapy corrects the abnormal adipose tissue; conservative complex decongestive therapy is the mainstay, combining graduated compression garments with manual lymphatic drainage
Encourage regular low-impact exercise, particularly aquatic exercise, to support mobility and lymphatic flow
Offer weight management for coexisting obesity while explaining that the affected gynoid depots resist dietary energy restriction
Consider liposuction using tumescent or water-jet-assisted techniques for durable reduction of the affected fat in selected patients
Provide pain management and psychological support, addressing the tenderness, easy bruising and body-image impact
Monitor for progression to lipo-lymphoedema and treat secondary lymphatic insufficiency with intensified decongestive therapy
Advise attentive skin care to prevent complications in oedematous limbs
